newsitem.title: USA: KeyCorp Q4 revenue growth seen 5-6 pct.
newsitem.headline: KeyCorp Q4 revenue growth seen 5-6 pct.

text.p: KeyCorp may face challenges to rapid revenue growth as it pares branches in its drive to become a nationwide bank, but analysts said they see fourth quarter revenues up five to six percent from a year ago.
That would be in line with the industry, they added. KeyCorp expects to report its fourth quarter Thursday.

"I think (revenue growth) will probably be in the range of five to six percent year over year... pretty much in line with their experience for their first three quarters," McDonald & Co analyst Fred Cummings said.
First Call said analysts expect Key to report $0.98 a share fourth-quarter earnings versus the year-ago $0.86. For full-year 1996 and 1997, estimates were $3.72 and $4.24 versus $3.45 in 1995.
Cummings said Tuesday he sees 1996 earnings at $3.43 after a previously announced fourth-quarter restructuring charge.

KeyCorp chief executive officer Robert Gillespie said last month he thinks the bank is capable of annual earnings growth of at least 12 percent for the next two to three years but is likely to have about five percent net revenue growth in 1997.
Going forward, Cummings said, if revenue growth opportunities were lost as branches closed, Key's streamlining of its sales organization could offset the effect.
"I really like this restructuring," Cummings said, adding that a sales organization that is consistent nationwide should be more effective than the old structure of 12 separate banks.

In November KeyCorp said it planned a fourth-quarter $100 million charge to prune 2,700 jobs and more than 140 branches in its effort to be a nationwide bank. At the time it said it planned to repurchase up to 12 million shares in 1997.
KeyCorp, whose $65 billion in assets make it the 14th largest U.S. bank, said the changes should have annualized earnings benefits of $110 million by 1997 yearend.
Cummings said KeyCorp's good cost control, astute balance sheet management, wise capital management and share buybacks should allow it to meet estimates through 1997.

He said KeyCorp has not gotten the jolt in revenue growth it expected when the old Cleveland-based Society Corp and Albany, N.Y.-based Key merged in 1994. But, he said, revenue growth has been in line with the industry.
Joe Morford of Alex. Brown & Sons sees improved 1997 revenue growth after slightly better fourth-quarter revenues.

"I think the company's been fairly internally focused in terms of integrating in the wake of the merger (and) preparing for the national bank structure," he said. "In 1997 we should see some better (revenue growth) momentum."

Joseph Duwan, an analyst who follows KeyCorp for Keefe Bruyette & Woods, said the bank's efforts to "reinvent itself" bode well for 1997 and 1998. He praised Key's innovative marketing and its focus on its balance sheet.
Acquisitions are not a likely priority in 1997 as Key uses capital for share buybacks, Morford said.
Duwan said if Key sought acquisitions, they would likely be in non-bank areas such as regional brokerages or home equity financing.
